headline: Six archetypes, thirty-six different Pokémon, every trainer slot its own agent seeing nothing but fog of war. Fifteen agents played and five refereed — and the referees confirmed four engine defects, one of which decided the final.

rules.label: The field
rules.text: Six teams, one archetype each: stall, hazard stack, glass cannon, sun, trick room, status. Level 50 singles, 6v6, standard clauses — species, item, evasion, OHKO and sleep. Thirty-six roster slots, thirty-six different Pokémon: no species appears on two teams.

rules.label: The agents
rules.text: Every trainer slot was a separate agent process. A fresh pilot took the seat each round, briefed on its roster and on exactly how its predecessor won or lost — including the mistake that predecessor named itself.

rules.label: The fog
rules.text: A player saw its own team in full and only the opponent's active Pokémon. Bench species stayed hidden until sent out, and the foe's ability and item stayed hidden until an event revealed them — enforced by the engine's own projection, not by instruction.

rules.label: The judge
rules.text: A third agent refereed each match: it watched every resolution, audited the engine against its own source, and filed defects to the organiser with a CONFIRMED / NOT-A-BUG / UNCERTAIN verdict on each.

rules.label: The clock
rules.text: Turn cap 60. A match still alive at the cap goes to a decision on Pokémon standing, then total HP. Both pilots were told the cap existed — a stall team that knows it is behind on the clock plays differently.

rules.label: The bracket
rules.text: Three Round 1 matches put all six on the board at once. The bye rule was announced before Round 1, not chosen after it: most Pokémon remaining, tiebreak fewest turns. The bye holder waited in the final while the other two winners fought for the right to face it.

byes.name: Guillotine Club
byes.reason: bye to the final — 4 Pokémon remaining was the most dominant Round 1 result, under a rule announced before Round 1 rather than chosen after it

standings.name: Guillotine Club
standings.summary: Champion, undefeated, and the only team never to lose a match. Beat stall by refusing to grind — one-shots only, because Regenerator and Roost refund anything less — and beat trick room with a +3-priority flinch the engine let it throw every single turn.

standings.name: The Low Ceiling
standings.summary: The only team to win twice on the field. Beat a hazard stack by refusing to switch and a sun team by banking its last setter at full HP, then met a priority move that no Trick Room can reorder and lost the final without its second Room scoring a single kill.

standings.name: Meridian
standings.summary: Swept a status team inside its eight turns of noon, then relit a second full sun off a switch its own dossier said was impossible — and still lost, because doubling your Speed is a liability when the room is upside down.

standings.name: The Caltrops
standings.summary: Laid the complete floor — rocks, a spike layer, both toxic layers — and took four bodies with it, the best Round 1 loss of the three. Never used Roar or Dragon Tail once, so nobody ever paid the entry tax twice.

standings.name: Miasma
standings.summary: Paralysed the sun setter on turn one and thereby locked itself out of its own 97%-accurate Sleep Powder, because a Pokémon may carry only one major status. Four-sixths Bug and Grass into Drought was the rest of it.

standings.name: Perish Row
standings.summary: Outsped by every Pokémon it faced, so every switch-in paid a full hit on entry and died before acting — a stall team that never gets a turn cannot stall. Perish Song never fired: Lapras died on turn 20 with all five PP unused.

god_notes:
## What the referees found

Four confirmed defects, from five refereed matches. Every one was investigated against engine source before it was filed, every one was re-verified by the organiser before it was touched, and every fix ships with a test demonstrated to fail on the unfixed code.

**Fake Out had no first-turn restriction, and it decided the final.** The dataset carries the move as priority +3 with a 100%-chance flinch and nothing else; `domain.Move` has no field that could express "first turn only"; and the string `fake-out` appeared in no Go file in the repository. The gate could not have been written without new state, so there was no gate. Both finalists found it independently on turn 13 — the losing pilot by reading `moves.json` *after* it had already cost a Pokémon — and the final's referee proved it by absence in three parts. Against a Trick Room team this is not chip damage: priority is the one thing Trick Room does not reorder, so Persian threw a guaranteed flinch on its fifth, sixth and seventh consecutive turns on the field, and the second Room — with four live Pokémon behind it — produced no kills at all. `Volatiles` now carries a `MoveActions` counter, incremented at the top of `executeMove` so a turn spent recharging or fully paralysed still burns the privilege, exactly as canon counts the action rather than the outcome.

**Trace never reverted, so it fired at most once per battle.** The engine assigned the copied ability in place with nothing remembering the original. A tracer that ever pivoted was locked to its first copy for the rest of the game — and wore, in the meantime, an ability it had no legal claim to. The semifinal's referee caught it watching Porygon copy Flame Body, switch out, and come back opposite a Drought Ninetales still holding Flame Body. `Pokemon` now carries `BaseAbility`, restored on switch-out. The final's referee confirmed the fix in live play: Porygon copied Technician on its first entry and Lightning Rod on its second.

**Effect Spore ignored powder immunity.** Since Gen VI it is a powder effect — Grass types, Overcoat and Safety Goggles are immune. The engine *had* that immunity and could not reach it: `powderRefusedBy` opens by testing the *move's* powder flag, and the move that triggers the ability rider is the attacker's contact move, which carries no such flag. The guard returned "not refused" every time. The three immunities now live in `powderImmuneBy`, which asks about a Pokémon rather than about a move aimed at one. The check deliberately sits *after* both of the rider's RNG rolls, so the stream is unchanged and old replays stay valid.

**Five abilities were documented as inert and registered as working.** `abilities.go` groups its registry under two headings that mean opposite things, and `neutralizing-gas`, `forewarn`, `illuminate`, `run-away` and `healer` sat under "hook-free but fully functional" while the same file's comment twenty lines above listed them as inert. This is the most expensive kind of wrong, because it is the kind a reader acts on: a referee read the heading, concluded Neutralizing Gas worked, and The Caltrops spent a Pokémon switching Weezing in to suppress an ability that has no suppression code anywhere in the repository. The engine behaved correctly throughout; only its description of itself was false. A test now pins the documentation against the registrations in both directions.

The referees cleared far more than they confirmed, which is the right ratio. Between them they hand-recomputed damage rolls across the full modifier chain in every match, and two caught themselves mid-accusation with a wrong constant — one had transcribed Life Orb as 5324/4096 where `toMod` deliberately rounds to nearest and gives 5325. Cleared with citations: the whole weather chain including Heat Rock's eight turns and the final-turn residual ordering; Trick Room on every axis (−7 priority, five ticks including the setting turn, a second cast ending rather than extending it, inversion applied to the fully modified Speed so paralysis and Chlorophyll compose correctly); Technician's ≤60 gate proven in both directions on the same Persian on adjacent turns; hazard layer scaling and the hazards→ability→item switch-in order; Guts and burn sharing a single predicate so the Attack cut cannot double-count; Skill Link stopping on a faint without rolling a flinch into a corpse; and two damage figures in the final that are only reachable with Showdown's round-half-down bias.

## What I got wrong

**The team names leak the archetype.** The harness prints `"Your opponent is The Low Ceiling — their roster and archetype are hidden"`, which is a sentence that refutes itself. Every name I chose is a tell: Perish Row, The Caltrops, Guillotine Club, Miasma, Meridian, The Low Ceiling. The champion said so plainly — *"the team name gave away the archetype before turn one, so I led into the room instead of switching"* — and removed Mr. Mime on turn 2. This is the direct descendant of last run's theme-string leak. That hole was in the harness and got fixed; I then reopened it through naming, which no code change can close. Next run: names that describe nothing, or a display name distinct from the roster's identity.

**I built a team around an ability the engine does not implement.** Meridian's roster blurb promises that "Harvest keeps handing the berry back". Harvest is registered inert — no hooks at all — so Exeggutor's Sitrus Berry is one-and-done, and the theme string its own pilot reads before turn one is false. The Round 1 pilot caught it by reading source, demoted Exeggutor to a bench body and never sent it in; its successor inherited the correction. Meridian therefore played the whole tournament as a five-and-a-half Pokémon team, and that is on me, not on the engine — which documents the gap honestly in the same file I failed to read while building the roster. Per the runbook I did not touch a live roster to fix it.

**One dossier carried a false claim into a match.** Meridian's Round 1 pilot wrote that Ninetales' eight turns of sun "die with it". They do not — weather is a field state with its own countdown and survives its setter. The semifinal pilot inherited that sentence, read `setWeatherFromAbility`, found it wrong, and relit a second full eight turns by switching Ninetales back in on turn 10. The briefing chain repaired itself, but a pilot that trusted its dossier would have been worse off than one that had never read it. Dossiers are testimony, not documentation, and next run should say so in the prompt.

## What went right

The binary was rebuilt from current source before match one and again after the patches — the single line in the runbook that last run got wrong, and the reason every match here is replayable from its seed. Round 1 and the semifinal ran on `2390fb1`; the final ran on `72c0407`, after three of the four fixes landed. Every match is stamped with its revision, and no match ever ran on two.

The hand-checked colour note from last run is now `royale/palette_check.py`: WCAG contrast for each colour on its own ground, CIE76 ΔE between the two sides of each pairing. All fifteen team combinations clear, so no bracket outcome could have produced the yellow-against-orange final that broke the first assignment.

And the thing the exercise is actually for: thirty-six roster slots, thirty-six different Pokémon, no species shared between any two teams — and four real defects in an engine whose unit suite is green, found by agents reading live battle logs rather than fixtures written by someone who already believed the mechanic worked.
